case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal Election Day statutes (and related constitutional structure) preempt Mississippi’s rule allowing absentee ballots mailed by Election Day to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day in federal elections.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302 (formerly 2 U.S.C. §§ 7, 8) (federal Election Day statutes fixing the day for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors); U.S. Const. art. I, § 4 (Elections Clause) and art. II, § 1, cl. 4 (Presidential Electors Clause); Mississippi Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a) (ballot receipt deadline extension).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (through the Secretary of State) argues that its statute is consistent with federal law and constitutional design because voters still ‘choose’ federal officers on the federally prescribed Election Day when they cast or mail ballots by that day; allowing election officials to receive and count timely-cast ballots after Election Day is an administrative canvassing practice traditionally left to the States. Petitioner contends the Fifth Circuit misread Supreme Court precedent (especially Foster) by treating any post-Election-Day receipt window as extending the federal election itself, and warns that the decision threatens widespread state practices, risks voter disenfranchisement (e.g., mail delays), and creates instability close to national elections. Petitioner and supporting amici also invoke broader structural arguments under the Electors/Elections Clauses and later-enacted federal statutes (e.g., UOCAVA) to suggest Congress did not intend Election Day statutes to invalidate reasonable receipt rules.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (RNC and others) argue the federal Election Day statutes require a single, nationwide day for the final act of choosing federal officers, and Mississippi’s five-business-day post-Election-Day receipt deadline effectively extends the election period beyond that day. They contend that when a State counts ballots that arrive after Election Day, the ‘choice’ is not completed on Election Day, creating a legally impermissible multi-day election for federal offices. Respondents maintain the Fifth Circuit correctly applied Foster’s reasoning to hold the Mississippi receipt rule preempted, and they argue there is no Supreme Court decision approving post-Election-Day ballot receipt for general elections. They emphasize the stakes in close races and argue uniformity and predictability require enforcing Election Day as a hard deadline for receipt/counting, not merely for mailing or casting.
key_precedents: Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Democratic Nat’l Comm., 589 U.S. 423 (2020) (per curiam)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer, 199 F.3d 773 (5th Cir. 2000)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Keisling, 259 F.3d 1169 (9th Cir. 2001)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor make the best point that the federal Election Day statutes do not expressly require “receipt by Election Day,” and Foster declined to “isolate precisely what acts” must occur that day. But even taking that caution seriously, Foster’s central holding remains that Congress fixed a single day on which the State’s and voters’ actions must culminate in a legally operative “final selection,” and Mississippi’s rule makes legal effectiveness turn on post-Day receipt rather than post-Day counting of ballots already validly received. Justice Jackson’s disenfranchisement concern is substantial, yet under a minimalist, institution-protective approach I would resolve only the narrow conflict: States may process and canvass after Election Day, but they may not add newly eligible federal ballots based on an event occurring after the congressionally fixed day absent clearer congressional authorization. RNC v. DNC does not answer the statutory question, but it underscores the judiciary’s limited role and the systemic value of stable, uniform temporal rules—supporting a restrained holding confined to federal contests.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor correctly note that §§ 20301–20302 do not spell out “receipt by Election Day,” and Foster declined to catalogue every required act on that day. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, Foster still fixes the controlling principle: the State’s and voters’ combined actions must culminate in a legally operative “final selection” on the congressionally chosen day, and Mississippi’s rule makes a ballot legally effective only upon receipt—an event that can occur after that day—thereby enlarging the set of eligible federal votes beyond the single federal ‘day.’ Calling receipt “administrative” (Justice Kagan) fails under a textual/original public meaning approach because the legal line between eligible and ineligible ballots is itself substantive, not mere canvassing of already-valid votes. Disenfranchisement concerns (Justice Jackson) are serious, but they cannot justify reading Congress’s single-day command as a multi-day election window absent textual authorization.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that §§ 20301–20302 do not expressly say “receipt by Election Day,” and Foster declined to specify every act that must occur that day; but that caution does not erase Foster’s operative premise, emphasized by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas, that the State’s and voters’ combined actions must culminate in a legally operative “final selection” on the congressionally fixed day. Mississippi’s scheme makes a ballot legally effective only upon receipt, which may occur after Election Day, thereby expanding the set of eligible federal votes after the federal deadline rather than merely canvassing votes already made effective on the day. Justice Jackson’s disenfranchisement concern is serious, but under a textualist approach it cannot supply authority to convert Congress’s single “day” into a multi-day receipt window absent clearer congressional authorization. The administrability and uniformity interests noted by the Chief Justice reinforce that line: States remain free to facilitate voting through earlier mailing deadlines, drop boxes, and in-person options, but they cannot make post-Day receipt the condition that creates a valid federal vote.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh offer the cleanest limiting principle—post–Election Day “receipt” (unlike canvassing) determines legal effectiveness and thus extends the “final selection” beyond the federal day—but that reads Foster as silently constitutionalizing a receipt-by-midnight rule that its own cautionary language rejects. Foster condemned a scheme that fixed the decisive choice before Election Day and expressly declined to “isolate precisely what acts” must occur on that day; absent clearer congressional text in §§ 20301–20302, I cannot infer a disenfranchising preemption rule from that ambiguity. Mississippi’s statute makes voter eligibility turn on the voter’s timely act by Election Day (mailing/postmark) and uses a short receipt window to account for postal delay; treating delivery timing as the legally operative moment elevates administrative happenstance over the voter’s compliance and predictably burdens voters with less access to reliable mail. RNC v. DNC’s institutional-stability concerns, which the Chief invokes, do not supply the missing statutory clarity to displace state election administration on a close Elections Clause preemption question.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the administrable line they draw between post–Election Day canvassing and post–Election Day receipt, arguing that receipt is the “legally operative” moment and thus extends the election beyond the federally fixed day under Foster. But Foster both addressed a materially different scheme (one that effectively finalized the outcome before Election Day) and expressly declined to “isolate precisely what acts a State must cause to be done” on that day—cautioning against turning §§ 20301–20302 into an implicit receipt-by-midnight rule without clearer text. On a pragmatic textualist view, Mississippi can coherently define the voter’s operative act as timely casting by Election Day (here, timely mailing), treating later receipt as part of post-Day administration much like the post-Day tabulation and canvass Foster contemplates, so the conflict is not clear enough to warrant preemption. Justice Alito’s uniformity concerns are weighty, but they function as policy reasons for Congress to specify a receipt deadline, not as a textual basis for us to supply one through conflict-preemption.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the best point: §§ 20301–20302 do not expressly say “receipt by Election Day,” and Foster declined to specify every act required that day. But Chief Justice Roberts’s framing, echoed by Justice Kavanaugh, fits Foster’s controlling premise: Congress fixed a single day on which the State’s and voters’ actions must culminate in a legally operative “final selection,” and Mississippi’s rule makes legal effectiveness turn on a post-Day event—receipt—thereby enlarging the set of eligible federal ballots after the federal day has passed. Calling receipt “administrative” (Justice Kagan) does not answer the legal question, because under Mississippi law receipt is the condition that creates a countable vote, unlike post-Day canvassing of ballots already timely received. Justice Jackson’s disenfranchisement concerns are real, but under a textualist/originalist separation-of-powers approach they cannot supply the missing congressional authorization for a multi-day federal election window.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s and Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that §§ 20301–20302 never say “receipt by Election Day” and that Foster declined to “isolate precisely what acts” must occur that day—highlights genuine statutory ambiguity. But as Chief Justice Roberts frames it, Foster still supplies a controlling limiting principle for institutional, precedent-based judging: Election Day is the federal boundary for when a State may make additional ballots legally eligible to affect the federal count, even if canvassing and tabulation continue afterward. Mississippi’s scheme makes legal effectiveness hinge on post-Day receipt, which is not mere post-Day “administration” but an expansion of the set of countable federal votes after the congressionally fixed day, creating the kind of timing clash Foster treats as impermissible. Justice Jackson’s disenfranchisement concerns are weighty, yet under our separation-of-powers approach they argue for Congress to adjust the rule rather than for us to dilute the uniform-day command through conflict-avoidance when the State’s own law makes receipt the decisive validity event.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor press the best point that §§ 20301–20302 do not expressly say “receipt by Election Day,” and Foster declined to specify every act that must occur on that day. But Chief Justice Roberts’s framing captures why the conflict is still real: Mississippi’s rule makes legal effectiveness of a federal vote depend on an event—receipt—that may occur after the congressionally fixed day, thereby enlarging the set of eligible federal ballots after Election Day rather than merely counting ballots already timely received. Under the ordinary public meaning of a single fixed “day” for holding the election, and Foster’s operative “final selection” boundary, post-Day canvassing is permissible while post-Day eligibility-creating receipt is not. Justice Jackson’s disenfranchisement concerns are serious, yet under an originalist/textualist approach they cannot supply the clear congressional authorization needed to transform a single-day federal election into a multi-day receipt window.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s clearest point is their administrability line: post–Election Day canvassing is permissible, but post–Election Day receipt allegedly expands the set of legally countable votes and thus extends the “final selection” beyond the federal day under Foster. Under my methodology, that line is not compelled by §§ 20301–20302’s text, and Foster’s refusal to “isolate precisely what acts” must occur on Election Day makes it a weak foundation for inferring a rigid receipt-by-midnight condition that would override longstanding state choices defining timeliness by the voter’s compliance on Election Day. Justice Thomas’s framing that “receipt” is necessarily the legally operative moment assumes what must be shown: Mississippi can reasonably treat mailing by Election Day as the operative act and later receipt as administrative completion, so the conflict is not “clear” enough to justify disenfranchising preemption. The uniformity/uncertainty concerns Roberts and Kavanaugh raise are serious, but absent a clearer congressional command, I would not read federal silence to displace a State’s procedural-fairness judgment aimed at mitigating postal happenstance.

John Roberts.reasoning: Congress has fixed a uniform day for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302, and under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause that federal timing rule preempts contrary state rules. In Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), we construed “Election Day” as the “combined actions of voters and officials meant to make a final selection of an officeholder,” and Mississippi’s rule permitting counting of ballots first received after that day extends the State’s participation in the final selection beyond the federally prescribed date. While States retain broad authority over election “mechanics,” that authority operates only “so far as Congress declines to preempt,” Foster, 522 U.S. at 69, and a narrow holding here would invalidate only post–Election Day receipt for federal elections while leaving States free to accommodate voters through earlier mailing deadlines or other on-day methods. Given the importance of predictable, nationally uniform federal election timing (especially in close contests) and the lack of clear congressional authorization for post-day receipt windows, I would affirm preemption on these facts.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302, fix a single day for the election of Representatives and Presidential electors, and the original public meaning of a congressionally prescribed “day for the election” is a single, determinate day on which the choice is made. Under Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), the “final selection” of federal officers must occur on that federally fixed day; Mississippi’s rule that treats ballots arriving after Election Day as timely effectively allows part of the legally operative act of choosing (ballot receipt and inclusion in the count) to occur after the day Congress set, contrary to the statute’s text and uniformity purpose. While States retain authority over election “Times, Places and Manner” under Art. I, § 4 and Art. II, § 1, cl. 4, that power is subject to Congress’s superior authority, and Congress has exercised it here by specifying the election day. Administrative canvassing may occur after Election Day, but counting ballots that were not received by Election Day extends the election beyond the day Congress mandated and is therefore preempted.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Congress, exercising its express authority under the Elections Clause and the Presidential Electors Clause, fixed a single national “day” for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors. 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302 and 3 U.S.C. § 1 are best read to require that the decisive act of election administration—receipt and acceptance of ballots for counting—be completed by Election Day; Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt window therefore creates an impermissible multi-day federal election. Foster v. Love supports this understanding by treating federal Election Day as a hard temporal boundary that preempts state rules effectively extending the election beyond that day, and the practical consequences of post-Day receipt (uncertainty in close races and diminished uniformity) reinforce that conclusion. While States retain broad authority over “manner,” that authority cannot conflict with Congress’s chosen “time,” and Mississippi’s statute (Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a)) conflicts with the federal time requirement as applied to federal contests.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302, fix a uniform day for the act of "choosing" Representatives and Presidential electors, but they do not clearly mandate that States may not count ballots that were timely cast/mailed by that day and received shortly thereafter pursuant to state law. Foster v. Love held preempted a scheme that effectively completed the election before the federally prescribed day, while expressly declining to "isolate precisely what acts a State must cause to be done" on federal election day, leaving room for States’ traditional authority over canvassing and tabulation administered after Election Day. Given that Mississippi’s rule turns on voter action by Election Day and operates as a modest receipt/canvassing window, I would not infer preemption absent unmistakable congressional direction, particularly where the practical effect of a hard receipt deadline would predictably disenfranchise voters facing mail delays and other barriers. This approach is also consistent with the caution expressed in Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Democratic Nat’l Comm. (2020) about disruptive last-minute rules, and with the Elections Clause’s baseline that States run elections subject to clear congressional override.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, fix a uniform day for the electorate’s act of “choosing” federal officers, but they do not clearly speak to (or forbid) a State’s administrative rule treating ballots timely cast/mailed by that day as valid though received shortly afterward. Foster v. Love held preempted a regime that allowed the decisive election to occur before the federally specified day, but its “final selection” language is best read to ensure the choice is made on Election Day—not to constitutionalize a hard receipt deadline when the voter’s act required by state law (mailing by Election Day) occurs on that day. Given the States’ traditional authority over “Times, Places and Manner” under Art. I, § 4, and the workability problems and disruption to widespread practices that a contrary rule would create, Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt window is not preempted absent a clearer congressional command. Republican Nat’l Comm. v. Democratic Nat’l Comm. underscores that Election Day disputes centrally concern when ballots are cast, and nothing in the federal text compels treating brief post-Day receipt as extending the election itself.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix a single day for the “election” of Representatives (52 U.S.C. § 20301) and for appointing presidential electors (3 U.S.C. § 1), and the ordinary meaning of “election” in this context is the “final selection” of the officeholder on that day. In Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67, 71–72 (1997), we read these statutes to require that the combined actions of voters and officials culminate in a final choice on Election Day, rejecting state rules that effectively create a nonuniform federal election period outside the congressionally set day. Mississippi’s scheme authorizes counting ballots that become legally operative only upon receipt after Election Day, which extends the State’s “final selection” beyond the federally prescribed day and thus conflicts with Congress’s Elections Clause/Presidential Electors Clause authority to set the time of choosing. Where Congress has spoken in clear temporal terms, state “administrative” practices cannot move the completion of the federal choice to a later day, especially given the structural interest in a uniform national Election Day.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Congress, exercising its express Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause authority, fixed a single nationwide "day" for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors. See 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302; U.S. Const. art. I, § 4; art. II, § 1, cl. 4. Under Foster v. Love, the federal statutes require that the final act of choosing occur on that day, and a state regime that treats legally effective votes as being cast/received after Election Day risks creating the sort of non-uniform, extended election period Congress sought to foreclose. Because Mississippi’s rule makes ballots arriving after Election Day eligible to be counted in federal elections, it conflicts with the federally prescribed temporal deadline and is therefore preempted.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix “the day” for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors, see 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302, and under the Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause Congress’s time-setting choice is controlling over contrary state rules. In Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), this Court read those statutes to require that the “final act” of choosing federal officers occur on the federally prescribed day, preempting a state scheme that effectively made the decisive choice outside Election Day. Mississippi’s rule, by permitting ballots to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day, similarly extends the legally operative event beyond the uniform day Congress selected, creating a conflict with federal law and thus preemption. While States retain broad authority over election administration, that discretion does not include redefining the temporal boundary Congress fixed for the federal election itself.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20301–20302, fix a uniform day for choosing federal officers, but they do not clearly speak to (or forbid) States’ longstanding administrative practice of receiving and tabulating timely-cast ballots after Election Day. Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), held that a State may not "consummate" the election prior to the federally prescribed day; it also recognized that key election mechanics occur before and after Election Day, and it did not decide whether counting ballots mailed by Election Day but received shortly thereafter is preempted. Given the serious practical risk of disenfranchisement from mail delays and the absence of unambiguous congressional direction to make receipt-by-Election-Day a hard federal requirement, I would not find conflict preemption here under the Elections Clause/Presidential Electors framework. Procedural fairness and equal access concerns counsel against reading the Election Day statutes to invalidate Mississippi Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a) absent a clearer statement from Congress.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal “Election Day” statutes preempt Mississippi’s law permitting valid absentee ballots mailed by Election Day to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day in federal general elections.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Federal Election Day statutes governing the “time” of congressional and presidential elections (e.g., 2 U.S.C. § 7 for Representatives; 2 U.S.C. § 1 for presidential electors), implicated alongside the Constitution’s Elections Clause (Art. I, § 4) and Presidential Electors Clause (Art. II, § 1, cl. 4), as applied to Mississippi’s receipt-deadline statute, Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Mississippi (through the Secretary of State) argues its ballot-receipt rule does not extend the “time” of the federal election beyond Election Day because voters must cast/submit ballots by Election Day and the post–Election Day window merely accommodates delivery and processing of timely-cast ballots. Petitioner contends the Fifth Circuit misread Supreme Court precedent (especially Foster) and overextended the federal Election Day statutes to regulate routine post-election administration. Petitioner also emphasizes Congress’s broader election framework (including UOCAVA) and historical practice, arguing it is implausible Congress meant “Election Day” statutes to impede voting by invalidating ballots timely cast but delayed in transit. Petitioner warns the decision below has disruptive, nationwide consequences for established mail-voting systems and invites uncertainty in close elections.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the federal Election Day statutes set a uniform, single day on which the election for federal offices must be consummated, and a state cannot keep the election ‘open’ by counting ballots that arrive after that day. In their view, allowing receipt-and-counting after Election Day effectively extends the election period and conflicts with federal law, triggering preemption. They maintain the Fifth Circuit correctly applied Foster’s reasoning to conclude that an election is not ‘consummated’ while late-arriving ballots can still be added, and they distinguish cases cited by Mississippi as not addressing general-election post–Election Day ballot receipt. Respondents also downplay the need for immediate Supreme Court intervention, arguing the legal question can continue to percolate and that petitioner overstates the decision’s sweeping impact.
key_precedents: Republican National Committee v. Democratic National Committee, 589 U.S. 423 (2020) (per curiam)
Voting Integrity Project, Inc. v. Bomer, 199 F.3d 773 (5th Cir. 2000)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito press the hardest point: that a single federally fixed “day” is diluted if additional legally operative votes may enter the count after that date, and they invoke Foster’s “consummated” language to treat any post-Day receipt as unlawful vote accretion. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett emphasize, §§ 7 and 1 do not speak in receipt terms, and I am not prepared—consistent with minimalism and clear-statement principles in federal-state allocation—to convert general “day” language into implied preemption of state manner rules where the voter timely cast the ballot by Election Day and only mail delivery and counting occur after. Foster remains persuasive against schemes that effectively complete the election before the federal day; extending its “consummated” phrasing to mandate nationwide receipt-by-Election-Day would read beyond its holding and beyond what Congress clearly enacted. Narrowly, I would hold federal law fixes the deadline for casting a ballot on Election Day, while leaving reasonable post-Day receipt and counting of timely cast ballots to the States absent more specific congressional direction.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Barrett’s best point is that §§ 7 and 1 do not expressly mention “receipt” and that Foster arose in the early-election context, but that focus understates the statutory text Congress did choose: a single nationwide “day” on which the election is “held.” Under Foster’s understanding that the election must be “consummated” on that day, Mississippi’s rule is not mere post-day tabulation; it keeps the set of legally countable votes open after the federal date by treating later-arriving ballots as timely votes. Justice Kagan’s “timely cast” reframing depends on equating postmark with voting for federal-law purposes, yet the ordinary public meaning of “holding” an election fixes when votes may be received as legally operative choices, not when the State later decides to deem them effective. Reliance and burden concerns (Justice Sotomayor; Justice Kavanaugh) may bear on remedy, but they cannot rewrite Congress’s one-day command into an open-ended period without a clearer textual basis than “day.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s minimalist distinction between “casting” by Election Day and later “receipt” is the strongest point on the other side, but it effectively rewrites Congress’s choice of a single uniform “day” for the election into a rule that the legally operative electorate may keep expanding after that day. Foster’s statement that the election must be “consummated” on the federal day is not limited to “early election” schemes; as Justice Gorsuch notes, the same textual problem arises when a State keeps the set of countable ballots open after Election Day rather than merely counting ballots already received. Justice Kagan’s reliance on longstanding absentee practice and the statutes’ lack of an express receipt clause cannot overcome the ordinary meaning of “the day” as a fixed temporal endpoint when the practical consequence is delayed finality and interstate disuniformity in when the choice is settled. Justice Barrett’s clear-statement federalism concern is weighty in close cases, but here the conflict is direct: a one-day federal election cannot be administered as a multi-day acceptance period for new, legally effective votes.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that a single federally fixed “day” is undermined if the universe of countable ballots can expand after that day—deserves engagement, but it depends on equating “receipt” with the legally operative act of “voting” without a clear congressional directive. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Foster’s “consummated” language responded to an election effectively completed before Election Day; extending it to impose an implied receipt-by-Election-Day mandate stretches §§ 7 and 1 beyond their text and would displace traditional state “manner” choices absent clear conflict. Under my pragmatic approach, construing the statutes to invalidate ballots timely cast (postmarked) by Election Day would predictably disenfranchise lawful voters for mail delays outside their control, a severe real-world consequence we should not infer from general “day” language. Justice Gorsuch’s finality concerns sound in policy and election administration, but they do not supply the kind of direct textual collision required for Supremacy Clause preemption here.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that the set of legally operative votes cannot expand after the federally fixed “day”—is intuitively appealing, but it depends on equating “vote acceptance/receipt” with when the election is “held,” which §§ 7 and 1 do not say. As Chief Justice Roberts notes, Foster condemned a scheme that effectively completed the election before the federal day; extending Foster’s “consummated” language to require receipt-by-Election-Day reads an additional cutoff into text that is silent on receipt and that has long coexisted with post-day administration of timely cast absentee ballots. Justice Gorsuch’s “universe of votes” framing proves too much under a pragmatic textualist approach because it would treat ordinary mail delivery and canvassing—after a voter has timely acted—as unlawful vote “accretion,” displacing state manner rules without a clearer congressional command. Absent an explicit federal receipt deadline, the more coherent line is that Election Day fixes the deadline for casting, while reasonable rules for receiving and counting timely cast ballots remain with the States.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan offer the strongest pushback: §§ 7 and 1 do not expressly mention a receipt deadline and Foster arose in an “early election” regime. But under a textualist/originalist reading, Congress’s choice of a single federal “day” for choosing Representatives and electors is best understood—consistent with Foster’s “consummated” language—as fixing the moment by which the set of legally operative votes must be determined, even if counting continues afterward. Mississippi’s rule does not merely involve post-day tabulation of ballots already in hand; it authorizes additional ballots to become timely votes after the federally fixed day, effectively converting the election from a day to a period. Justice Barrett’s clear-statement federalism concerns are weighty, yet the clear statement here is Congress’s imposition of a uniform election “day,” and separation-of-powers principles counsel that any softer, policy-driven rule about mail delays must come from Congress, not our redefinition of “day.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch’s and Justice Alito’s best point is that Mississippi’s rule lets the universe of countable ballots expand after Election Day, and they rely on Foster’s “consummated” language to treat that as an irreconcilable conflict with §§ 7 and 1. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Foster addressed a scheme that effectively completed voting before the federal day; extending its rhetoric to infer a nationwide receipt-by-Election-Day mandate reads more into “the day” the election is “held” than the text clearly supplies and would impliedly preempt a traditional state “manner” choice about when an absentee ballot is cast (postmarked by Election Day). The opposing view also risks collapsing ordinary post-day ministerial processes into a federal prohibition whenever outcomes remain contingent—an approach that, in my institutionalist methodology, requires a clearer congressional statement before we displace widespread state practice and invite election-administration disruption. I therefore continue to view Election Day as the deadline for casting a ballot, while brief post-day receipt windows for timely cast ballots remain permissible absent more specific federal direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that a post–Election Day receipt window lets the universe of counted ballots “grow” after the congressionally fixed day, and they lean on Foster’s “consummated” language to treat that as a direct conflict. But as Chief Justice Roberts notes, Foster’s holding addressed a regime that effectively concluded the election before the federal day; extending its dictum to create an implied nationwide receipt-by-Election-Day rule goes beyond the text of 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, which fix a “day” for holding the election but do not specify when mailed absentee ballots must be received. On an original public meaning account, a ballot timely cast by Election Day (here, postmarked by that day under state law) can be treated as part of the election “held” on that day even though ministerial receipt, verification, and tabulation necessarily occur later, and preemption requires a clearer congressional command to displace state manner rules. The respondents’ “finality/consummation” framing has intuitive appeal, but it effectively equates “receipt” with “voting” and reads a uniform receipt deadline into statutory silence, which is not a move an originalist textualist methodology can justify.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito’s strongest point—that a single nationally fixed “day” cannot tolerate any post-Day accretion of countable ballots—depends on equating “vote acceptance/receipt” with the legally operative act of voting, and on reading Foster’s “consummated” language as silently imposing a receipt-by-Election-Day rule. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Foster addressed an election scheme that effectively ended voting before the federal day; extending it to invalidate ballots timely cast (postmarked) by Election Day would transform ordinary post-election administration into broad implied preemption without a clear congressional statement in 2 U.S.C. § 7 or 3 U.S.C. § 1. Justice Gorsuch’s “new votes entering the pool” framing is forceful, but under a procedural-fairness, pragmatic lens the relevant “pool” is the set of ballots timely cast by the federal deadline; later receipt and tabulation are ministerial steps that inevitably occur after the day and cannot, without clearer statutory text, justify disenfranchising timely voters based on mail latency. I therefore remain with the Petitioner: absent an express federal receipt deadline, states may treat a ballot as cast by Election Day and count it when received within a reasonable window.

John Roberts.reasoning: The federal “Election Day” statutes (2 U.S.C. § 7; 2 U.S.C. § 1; 3 U.S.C. § 1) fix the day on which voters must make their choice, but they do not clearly regulate a State’s ordinary post–Election Day administration for timely cast absentee ballots, and we should not lightly infer broad preemption in an area traditionally left to the States under the Elections Clause. Foster v. Love preempted a scheme that effectively concluded the election before the congressionally prescribed day; it did not hold that an election is unlawfully “extended” whenever States count timely cast ballots received shortly after Election Day. Given the statutes’ silence on receipt deadlines and the significant reliance interests in longstanding absentee-ballot practices, a narrow reading that allows Mississippi’s postmarked-by–Election Day rule avoids unnecessary disruption and better preserves institutional legitimacy. Respondents’ approach would extend Foster beyond its holding and convert general “time of election” language into a sweeping federal rule displacing diverse, established state procedures without a clear congressional command.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix the “day” for choosing Representatives and Presidential electors—2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—requiring a single, uniform time for the federal election as a matter of text and original public meaning. Under Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67 (1997), Congress mandated that the election be “consummated” on that day, even if ancillary administration occurs before or after; a state may not keep the election open by continuing to accept votes after the federally set day. Mississippi’s rule, Miss. Code Ann. § 23-15-637(1)(a), allows ballots to be received and counted after Election Day, which conflicts with the federal requirement that the election for federal offices occur on the appointed day and is therefore preempted under the Supremacy Clause. The Elections Clause and Presidential Electors Clause permit Congress to set that uniform time, and when Congress has done so, state law must yield.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes fix a single, nationally uniform "day for the election" of Representatives and presidential electors. See 2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1. Under Foster v. Love, 522 U.S. 67, 71–72 (1997), the "election"—the final choice of the electorate—must be "consummated" on that day, and a state regime that continues to accept and count ballots received after Election Day keeps the election open past the federally designated time, creating a direct conflict and thus preemption. While States retain substantial administrative authority under the Elections Clause and Electors Clause, that authority cannot be exercised to extend the period during which additional votes may be added after Election Day, particularly given the practical risks and uncertainty that follow from post-day receipt windows.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The federal "Election Day" statutes (2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1) set the day on which voting for federal offices must occur, but they do not clearly regulate routine post-election administration such as the receipt, canvassing, and tabulation of ballots timely cast by that day. Foster v. Love held that a State may not "consummate" a federal election before Election Day, while also acknowledging that aspects of the electoral process necessarily occur before and after Election Day; Mississippi’s rule does not permit voting after Election Day, it merely counts ballots mailed by Election Day that arrive shortly thereafter. Reading the federal statutes to invalidate timely-cast absentee ballots because of mail delays would unjustifiably burden access to the franchise—especially for rural voters, voters with disabilities, and those facing logistical barriers—without a clear congressional command, and the disruption risk counsels against such a sweeping preemption. Consistent with the Elections Clause framework (Art. I, § 4) and Congress’s demonstrated ability to speak clearly when it wishes to displace state election mechanics, I would not extend Foster to treat this narrow receipt window as an unlawful extension of the election itself.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. § 7; 2 U.S.C. § 1; 3 U.S.C. § 1) fix a uniform day on which voters must cast ballots and the election is "held," but they do not clearly regulate the State’s back-end administration of timely cast votes, including a short receipt window for ballots mailed by Election Day. Foster v. Love held that a State may not make the federal election be "consummated" before the congressionally designated day, yet it also recognized that some election-related steps necessarily occur before and after Election Day; extending Foster’s anti-early-election rule to forbid counting ballots timely cast but delivered shortly after Election Day reads more into the text than Congress specified. Under the Elections Clause framework, absent a clear conflict, States retain authority over the “Times, Places and Manner” of elections, and Mississippi’s five-business-day receipt rule functions as a workably administrable manner regulation that does not alter the federally fixed time for voting. Given the lack of an unambiguous statutory command that "Election Day" is a hard receipt deadline, and in light of statutory coherence with Congress’s broader election regime accommodating absentee voting, I would reject preemption here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes—2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—set a uniform national day on which federal elections are to be “held,” and under Foster v. Love that means the combined actions of voters and officials must “make a final selection” on that day. Mississippi’s rule allowing ballots to be received and counted up to five business days after Election Day necessarily permits additional lawful votes to be added after the federally fixed day, so the electorate’s final selection is not consummated on Election Day as Congress prescribed. While States retain broad Elections Clause authority to regulate the “Times, Places and Manner” of congressional elections, that authority yields where Congress has exercised its power to fix the time of the election, and the conflict here triggers preemption. Neither general election-administration statutes nor longstanding state practice can override the specific, controlling federal command for a single Election Day reflected in §§ 7 and 1 as construed in Foster.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The federal Election Day statutes, 2 U.S.C. § 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1, set the day on which voters must make their choice for federal offices, but they do not clearly regulate state administrative rules for receiving and counting absentee ballots that were timely cast (mailed) by Election Day. Foster v. Love held that a State may not “consummate” a federal election before Election Day, while recognizing that some election-related activities necessarily occur before and after Election Day; it does not squarely decide whether a State may count ballots cast by Election Day but received shortly after. Given the absence of clear statutory text forbidding post–Election Day receipt of timely-cast absentee ballots, principles of judicial restraint and federalism under the Elections Clause counsel against finding preemption, especially where the rule is practically workable and aligns with widespread historical practice. Cases like RNC v. DNC (2020) underscore caution about judicially altering election rules close to elections, reinforcing that this is a question for Congress to address expressly if it wishes to displace state receipt-deadline regimes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of the federal “Election Day” statutes—2 U.S.C. §§ 1 and 7 and 3 U.S.C. § 1—sets a uniform day for holding federal elections, but it does not expressly regulate ballot-receipt deadlines or prohibit counting ballots that were timely cast by that day. Foster v. Love held that a State may not “consummate” an election before the federally prescribed day, while acknowledging that some election-related steps naturally occur before and after Election Day; that holding does not clearly extend to invalidate a State’s post–Election Day receipt and counting of ballots mailed by Election Day. Given the absence of a clear textual conflict and the presumption that States retain authority over the “Times, Places and Manner” of elections subject to Congress’s limited displacement under the Elections Clause, Mississippi’s rule can be understood as administering the counting of timely votes rather than extending the “time” of the election itself. Preemption here would require reading the Election Day statutes as silently dictating a nationwide receipt deadline, a methodological leap not compelled by their original public meaning or by Foster’s narrow rationale.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I would hold that the federal Election Day statutes (2 U.S.C. § 7; 3 U.S.C. § 1; and related provisions) do not preempt Mississippi’s rule counting absentee ballots that are timely cast/mailed by Election Day but received within a brief, defined post–Election Day window. Foster v. Love addressed a state scheme that effectively concluded and “consummated” the federal election before the congressionally set day; it does not compel the much broader conclusion that Congress also mandated a uniform national receipt deadline that would invalidate ballots timely cast on Election Day due to ordinary mail delays. Reading “time” of the election to include routine post-election administration would intrude on States’ Elections Clause authority (Art. I, § 4) absent a clearer statement from Congress, and would create serious practical harms by disenfranchising lawful voters for reasons unrelated to voter eligibility or timely casting of a ballot. The better construction treats Election Day as the uniform deadline for casting a ballot, while allowing States reasonable latitude in receiving and counting timely-cast ballots, consistent with Congress’s evident willingness elsewhere (e.g., UOCAVA-related frameworks) to accommodate state-law receipt rules rather than impose a categorical receipt-by-Election-Day mandate.
